Mumbai civic body, India’s richest, to open bond sales to retail buyers

The corporation plans to raise as much as 95 billion rupees ($1 billion) through municipal or green municipal bonds in one or more tranches.

Saikat Das

27 November, 2026 08:13 pm IST

Follow Us:

The government is encouraging local bodies to raise funds for roads, bridges and sewerage systems through bonds. | Abeer Khan/Bloomberg

Mumbai’s civic authority, India’s richest, plans to tap individual investors through future bond sales to help finance urban infrastructure projects.

“We want to open it for the retail investors as well,” Ashwini Bhide, commissioner of the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation, said at an event Friday. “Mumbaikars can very well participate in the whole growth story of Mumbai.”

Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government is encouraging local bodies to raise funds for roads, bridges and sewerage systems through bonds, as India seeks to develop a municipal debt market along the lines of the US. Public offerings of municipal bonds remain rare in India, with most such debt sold privately to institutional investors.

Show Full Article

The corporation overseeing India’s financial capital plans to raise as much as 95 billion rupees ($1 billion) through municipal or green municipal bonds in one or more tranches, Bloomberg News reported earlier.

Large institutional investors are expected to subscribe to BMC’s offering, which is set to launch soon, Bhide said. The authority would go for a public sale of bonds slowly in future issuances, she said.

Municipal bodies raised 10 billion rupees in local-currency debt in 2025, the most in at least nine years, according to data from the regulator going back to 2017. Around 7.6 billion rupees of notes have been issued so far this year.

How Turkey cited India-made BrahMos to take aim at Cyprus in letter to UNSC, UNGA members

In letter to UNSC and UNGA members on 4 Nov, Turkey argued that Cyprus’s expanding military cooperation with foreign powers was undermining stability in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Debdutta Chakraborty

27 November, 2026 07:56 pm IST

Follow Us:

-->

Facebook

X

LinkedIn

Email

Copy Link

Representational | EU (L) and Turkish (R) flags outside a hotel in Istanbul, Turkey on 4 May, 2016 | Murad Sezer/Reuters

Stay updated with ThePrint:

-->

New Delhi: Cyprus and India’s growing defence partnership has become the latest source of friction between New Delhi and Ankara, with Turkey raising concerns at the United Nations Security Council over the speculated sale of Indian-made BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles to the Mediterranean island.

No formal agreement for the sale of BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles has been announced as yet.

In a letter circulated to members of the UNSC and UNGA on 4 November, Turkey argued that Cyprus’s expanding military cooperation with foreign powers was undermining stability in the Eastern Mediterranean. It singled out, among other developments, procurement of BrahMos missiles.

Show Full Article

“Greek Cypriot leader Nikos Christodoulides’ visit to New Delhi in May 2026 resulted in the strengthening of bilateral strategic relations and reported arrangements concerning the procurement of BrahMos supersonic missiles with an estimated range of 650 km,” read the letter.

Issued by Murat Soysal, representing the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, the self-declared state in the island’s north recognised only by Ankara, the letter goes on to argue that, by opening the island to military facilities and operations involving the United States, Israel and France, the “Greek Cypriot administration” has “effectively turned Cyprus into a military hub serving the strategic interests of external powers and drawn it closer to conflicts beyond the region”.

It accused the Republic of Cyprus, which Turkey refers to as the “Greek Cypriot administration”, of disrupting regional stability through what it described as unilateral, bilateral and multilateral military activities.

Turkey alleged in its letter to the UNSC that BrahMos negotiations followed a visit to New Delhi in May 2026 by Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides, during which the two countries sought to deepen their strategic partnership. New Delhi has increasingly engaged with countries in the Mediterranean including Cyprus, Greece, Armenia and Egypt through defence diplomacy, military exercises and potential arms exports.

For India, these partnerships offer opportunities to expand its defence exports, diversify strategic relationships and establish a larger presence in regions beyond its immediate neighbourhood.

For Ankara, however, some of these relationships carry a more direct security implication. India’s defence cooperation with Armenia has been a particular source of concern for Turkey and its close regional ally, Azerbaijan. Since 2022, Armenia has emerged as a significant destination for Indian military equipment, including Akash air defence systems and Pinaka multiple-launch rocket systems.

The deterioration in India-Turkey relations was also shaped by Ankara’s support for Pakistan during the military confrontation between India and Pakistan following the Pahalgam terror attack and India’s decision to target terror infrastructure in Pakistan in response.

Reports of Pakistan using Turkish-origin kamikaze drones during the conflict were criticised in New Delhi. India’s expanding defence relationships with Armenia, Greece and Cyprus have also since become part of a wider strategic conversation about competing partnerships taking shape across the region.

Also Read: India-Cyprus elevate ties to strategic partnership, announce defence roadmap & connectivity dialogue

Why Cyprus matters The dispute over Cypriot territories is rooted in one of the Mediterranean’s longest-running political conflicts.

The island, located at the crossroads of Europe, Asia and West Asia has a predominantly Greek Cypriot population and a Turkish Cypriot minority. Its modern political history has been shaped by competing national aspirations, communal violence and repeated failures to negotiate a lasting settlement.

Cyprus gained independence from British colonial rule in 1960 under a constitutional arrangement designed to share power between its Greek and Turkish communities.

The crisis deepened in July 1974, when a coup backed by the Greek military junta sought to unite Cyprus with Greece, under a policy that came to be known as enosis . Turkey subsequently launched a military intervention, invoking its responsibilities under the 1960 Treaty of Guarantee. The treaty was signed by Cyprus, Turkey, Greece and the United Kingdom to safeguard the constitutional framework of the newly independent Republic of Cyprus. It prohibited both the island’s union with another state ( enosis ) and its partition ( taksim ).

It also designated Turkey, Greece and Britain as guarantor powers, granting them a conditional right to intervene if the treaty’s provisions were violated.

The intervention resulted in the division of the island. Large numbers of Greek Cypriots fled or were displaced from the north, while Turkish Cypriots moved from the south. Turkish forces continue to maintain a military presence in the northern part of the island.

In 1983, the northern part of the island declared itself the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, a state recognised only by Turkey.

The internationally-recognised Republic of Cyprus joined the European Union in 2004, although the EU’s body of law remains suspended in the northern part of the island, where the government in Nicosia does not exercise effective control.

Efforts to reunify the island have repeatedly failed. A United Nations-backed settlement proposal, known as the Annan Plan, was approved by Turkish Cypriots but rejected by Greek Cypriots in separate referendums in 2004.

The unresolved conflict continues to shape the island’s security policy and its relationship with Ankara.

Meanwhile, India’s growing engagement with Cyprus and Greece comes at a time when the Eastern Mediterranean has become an increasingly important arena for defence cooperation, energy competition and strategic diplomacy.

Israel, which has developed a close defence-industrial relationship with India, is another important partner in the region. India has also strengthened its engagement with Greece and Egypt through diplomatic exchanges and military cooperation.

(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)

Nvidia Blackwell chips turn up at Shanghai data centre linked to Alice Huang

The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia’s Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed.

Andy Lin ,  Mackenzie Hawkins  and  Kari Lindberg

27 November, 2026 07:49 pm IST

Follow Us:

-->

Facebook

X

LinkedIn

WhatsApp

Email

Copy Link

Representative image

Stay updated with ThePrint:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

-->

A pair of Chinese firms installed Nvidia Corp.’s powerful Blackwell semiconductors in a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, the woman at the heart of a controversy surrounding the US chipmaker.

The gear installed at the Yangtze River Delta Project included a GB300 NVL72 rack, among Nvidia’s most powerful products, according to a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November. Shanghai Shuoyao offered the hardware as collateral to obtain a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank, according to filings from the lender that were reviewed by Bloomberg News.

A second firm Shanghai Kezhan, controlled by a Tokyo-based parent, described a GB200 server — which also relies on Blackwell chips — at the facility. That description was provided in documents when it obtained a 90 million yuan loan in late 2025 from a finance-leasing firm wholly owned by a local Shanghai government agency.

Show Full Article

The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia’s Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. These processors were until recently Nvidia’s most powerful data center products, and they’ve always been illegal to ship to China without a US license.

President Donald Trump has explicitly said he doesn’t want these chips — which OpenAI and Anthropic PBC use to train their most cutting-edge models — going to the Asian country, at least for now. Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard two-meter-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms (3,300 pounds) and is about the size of a gigantic fridge.

Nvidia and its just-reinstated CEO have come under intense scrutiny in recent weeks for their failure to stop diversion of the company’s products to China, a shadow trade that US officials believe is worth billions of dollars.

It’s unclear how the GB300 rack made its way to the country, to Shanghai Shuoyao or to this specific site — described in local media as designed to house as many as 800,000 servers. By inputting the serial number for the product into a public warranty database, Bloomberg found that it was manufactured by Taiwan’s Gigabyte Technology Co., which assembles Nvidia chips into servers and racks. The database also provided a model name for the serial number, which matches a GB300 NVL72 server rack manufactured by the Taiwanese company.

This sort of gear often passes through several hands — including local distribution networks — before it’s installed in data centers. In many cases, products that were ultimately smuggled into China were originally sold to parties in unrestricted areas.  Bloomberg provided the rack’s serial number to Gigabyte, seeking information about to whom Gigabyte had originally sold the hardware and when. It declined to answer those questions, citing company policy. The firm “conducts all business in compliance with applicable laws and regulations,” a spokesperson said in an emailed statement. “All transactions are subject to our internal compliance requirements and the relevant laws and regulations in effect at the time.”

Shanghai Shuoyao — the company that procured the GB300 rack and offered it as collateral — is active at the data center linked to Alice Huang and also has significant overlap with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is under US investigation over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia chips to China, Bloomberg has reported. Shanghai Shuoyao, which hasn’t responded to Bloomberg queries over the past year, confirmed this month in a rare public statement that it is one of Megaspeed’s service providers, describing the partnership as “limited to ordinary commercial cooperation.”

Megaspeed, meanwhile, used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to describe its largest data center to investors, dubbing the site a “specific area” facility in an unnamed country. Bloomberg does not have evidence that Megaspeed itself diverted Nvidia hardware there, and Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing in response to the US probe. The company has not answered repeated queries about the Yangtze River Delta Project. Nor has Nvidia, which for years insisted that there was no black market for its products and didn’t respond to questions for this story.

The Trump administration this month put Megaspeed on a US trade blacklist, citing a significant risk of involvement in chip diversion.

Alice Huang in 2023 founded Megaspeed, a so-called neocloud that won a coveted stamp of approval from Nvidia within four days of its creation, and went on to become the chipmaker’s largest Southeast Asian customer. She also has ties to a number of companies that invested in the Yangtze River Delta Project, which counts Kang Wei as its president. Kang has been introduced at times as Alice Huang’s romantic partner, people familiar with the matter said.

It’s unclear how far along operators are in meeting their overall goal for that project, which at 800,000 servers would be on par with hyperscale facilities used by companies like OpenAI. It’s also unclear what mix of servers they plan to use. The parameters they’ve outlined in construction plans reviewed by Bloomberg — specifically, the total processing power as compared to the energy input — would be extremely difficult to satisfy with chips from Chinese companies such as Huawei Technologies Co.

Still, the smuggled hardware disclosed in the filings reviewed by Bloomberg is just a fraction of what they’d need. These documents only cover hardware offered as collateral for loans — providing a small snapshot of the operators’ ambitions, while also underscoring how some Chinese financial institutions, including with government ties, were aware that restricted hardware was getting into China and willing to lend capital on those assets.

Bloomberg was unable to reach the leasing company that lent money to Shanghai Kezhan, nor Shanghai Innovation Bank, which in addition to the money it lent Shanghai Shuoyao, also provided a 200 million yuan loan to another company called Shanghai Longjie, similarly with restricted Nvidia chips as collateral.

Shanghai Longjie — which has the same parent company as Shanghai Shuoyao — disclosed in documents filed to regulators that it has servers containing Nvidia’s earlier Hopper-generation chips, which are illegal to ship to China without Washington’s permission, Bloomberg reported this month. That hardware was manufactured by Super Micro Computer Inc. and Dell Technologies Inc. It’s unclear whether the shipments had US approval.

Those aren’t the only Hopper chips at the Yangtze River Delta Project. Shanghai Kezhan, the company that described the GB200 server in filings last year, also disclosed that it has 32 servers with H200 chips there. These products had a Gigabyte prefix in their model name, but the documents didn’t include serial numbers — making them harder to trace.

Shanghai Kezhan is headquartered about half a kilometer from the Yangtze River Delta Project, at the same commercial complex where Shanghai Shuoyao solicited engineers to work on Nvidia H100 and H200 chips — two restricted models. In February 2024, both of these firms added “imports and exports” to their business activities, according to data from Qizhidao, a company information provider.

The same month, Megaspeed’s original parent — the Chinese gaming giant 7Road — obtained 16.7% of Shanghai Kezhan via a subsidiary the gaming company bought from Alice Huang in 2019. The other 83.3% of Kezhan is ultimately owned by NeXPower Japan, according to Qizhidao. Japan’s official companies registry returned only one company named NeXPower, which was established in March 2025. Caixin, a Chinese business news outlet, said the Tokyo firm is controlled by Alice Huang.

Bloomberg has been unable to reach NeXPower for comment. Chinese-speaking staffers at the firm’s registered address wouldn’t confirm that was NeXPower’s office, and shut the door after Bloomberg News asked about their relationship with Alice Huang and Shanghai Kezhan. On the intercom was a message saying they are working and will not respond to media questions. The registered address of the company’s director appeared to be a vacated residence.

In May 2025, records compiled by Big Trade Data show, Shanghai Kezhan received a shipment worth $11 million, flown from Malaysia to Shanghai Pudong International Airport with the company as consignee.

The customs document described the shipment as “storage chassis,” referring to a structure that houses components of a storage server. But the product code it was assigned to was 847150, which denotes computing servers. The shipment’s unit price was $264,108, too costly for a storage chassis — but within the price range of servers powered by Nvidia’s Hopper chips.

Modi addressed pay packet of India’s factory workers. Why growth in wages has been stagnant

Discourse over stagnation in wage growth has predominantly focused on developments of the past 2-3 years. But analysing data over four decades reveals a more significant narrative.

Bidisha Bhattacharya

27 November, 2026 08:30 am IST

Follow Us:

-->

Facebook

X

LinkedIn

WhatsApp

Email

Copy Link

Representational | File photo of a migrant worker resting inside a textile loom | Francis Mascarenhas/Reuters

Stay updated with ThePrint:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

-->

New Delhi: Prime Minister Narendra Modi, addressing the FICCI annual general meeting (AGM) last Thursday, put a pointed question to business leaders: “Did you increase the salaries of your employees [despite the reduction in basic corporate tax]?”

In doing so, he directly addressed the stagnation in wage growth in the private sector. And the data corroborates his concerns.

In the fiscal year 2024-25, the average factory worker’s earnings were approximately Rs 2.28 lakh, reflecting a 5.3 percent increase over the previous year, the latest Annual Survey of Industries shows.

Show Full Article

However, with consumer prices rising by 4.6 percent year-on-year, the real wage increase was a mere 0.7 percent. In FY 2023-24, real wage growth was 0.1 percent, and in FY 2022-23, real wages declined.

Excluding the recovery from the pandemic-induced downturn, real wage growth has remained below 1 percent in five of the past six years.

Infographic: Shruti Naithani/ThePrint The political discourse over stagnation in wage growth has predominantly focused on the developments of the past two to three years. But the same survey has been monitoring India’s manufacturing sector since 1981-82. Analysing this data over four decades reveals that the stagnation in wage growth is not merely a consequence of the pandemic or a temporary anomaly; rather, it represents the latest phase in a prolonged, gradual transformation in how benefits are distributed within Indian manufacturing.

This disparity can be illustrated with a simple comparison: the garment worker and the oil refinery worker.

Also Read: Real wages grew just 0.01% over the last 5 years and contracted in Haryana & UP, Ind-Ra report finds

Four decades of a shrinking slice In the Indian economy, a worker employed in an oil refinery contributes approximately Rs 43.6 lakh in value annually. In contrast, a garment worker in factories located in Tiruppur or Noida contributes around Rs 5 lakh. Despite the refinery worker generating nearly nine times the economic value, their remuneration is only about two and a half times greater than that of the garment worker, with earnings of Rs 4.25 lakh compared to Rs 1.76 lakh of the refinery worker.

Every manufacturing facility generates value, defined as the difference between its sales revenue and its expenditures on raw materials, fuel, and machinery depreciation. Economists refer to this as net value added, and the allocation of this value between labour and capital has long been a central inquiry in the field.

In the early 1980s, wages for factory workers in India constituted approximately 30 percent of this value. Following the 1991 economic reforms, this proportion slipped into a prolonged decline, reaching a nadir of 10.6 percent in FY 2007-08. Subsequently, it recovered steadily over the next decade, reaching 18.9 percent in FY 2019-20, before declining again post-pandemic. In 2024-25, it stood at 16.5 percent. Over the same four decades, the share of net value added going to profits rose from about 23 percent to around 50 percent, according to calculations based on the Annual Survey of Industries.

Infographic: Shruti Naithani/ThePrint The transformation observed is partly attributable to modernisation. Indian factories have become significantly more capital-intensive than in 1981, with machinery now commanding a larger share of returns. This trend also illustrates the evolution of factory work.

In the fiscal year 2019-20, 38 percent of factory workers in India were employed through contractors rather than directly by firms. By FY 2024-25, this proportion increased to 42 percent.

Contract workers generally receive lower wages, get fewer benefits, and possess limited bargaining power. This dynamic explains how factories were able to increase their workforce by approximately 30 lakh workers between FY 2021-22 and FY 2024-25 without substantially increasing individual wages.

Why productivity doesn’t reach the pay packet Returning to the context of the refinery and garment factory, standard economic theory posits that a worker’s compensation is approximately equivalent to their contribution to output. As a result, industries with higher worker productivity should ideally offer higher wages.

However, Indian factories only partially adhere to this principle. The value added per worker across industries ranges from approximately Rs 5 lakh to over Rs 40 lakh, yet annual wages remain within a narrower range of approximately Rs 1.8 lakh to Rs 4.3 lakh. Notably, the industries employing the largest workforce, such as food processing, textiles, and apparel, offer wages below the national average.

Infographic: Shruti Naithani/ThePrint What accounts for the lack of responsiveness of wages to productivity?

Arthur Lewis, who was later awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, provided a definitive explanation in 1954. In his influential paper on “economic development with unlimited supplies of labour,” Lewis explained that in nations where a significant portion of the population remains engaged in low-productivity agricultural work, wages in modern industry are determined not by the output of a factory worker but by the potential earnings from agricultural work, supplemented by a modest premium to incentivise the transition. As long as this labour reserve persists, factories can continue hiring at approximately the same wage level, with the benefits of increased productivity accruing primarily to capital.

Wages begin to rise significantly only when this labour reserve is depleted, a phenomenon economists now refer to as the Lewis turning point.

India, with nearly half of its workforce still employed in agriculture, exemplifies Lewis’s model. This explains why wages in the refinery and garment sectors are comparable despite substantial differences in productivity: both sectors recruit from the same extensive pool of individuals whose alternative employment is small-scale farming or casual labour.

Lifting the floor and the ladder The Lewis model provides a pathway for economic advancement. The primary strategy involves accelerating the transition of workers from low-productivity agriculture to manufacturing and service sectors, which can accommodate them on a large scale. This shift tightens the labour market for those remaining in agriculture, thereby exerting upward pressure on wages. Labour-intensive sectors such as apparel, footwear, and food processing, where India holds a comparative advantage, are expected to generate the majority of these employment opportunities.

The second strategy focuses on enhancing productivity within industries that currently employ the largest workforce. If workers in the garment and food-processing sectors could achieve productivity levels closer to the national average, there would be greater potential for wage increases.

This requires investment in advanced machinery, expansion of factory capacity, and stronger export market linkages, all of which can be facilitated by India’s recent trade agreements.

The third strategy is to establish a minimum wage. The four labour codes, effective since 21 November, 2025, provide for a national floor wage to reduce the disparity between contract workers and directly employed workers. If set judiciously, this can raise the lower end of the pay scale without causing job losses. Additionally, the codes’ provisions on contract labour aim to reduce the disparity between contract workers and directly employed workers. A year on, implementation is still catching up. By October this year, only six states and Union Territories had notified rules under all four codes, and the national floor wage itself is yet to be notified.

Furthermore, the Ministry of Statistics’ inaugural household income survey, currently underway, will provide comprehensive data on income trends across various employment types, addressing a longstanding gap in policymaking.

India’s economic narrative has traditionally focused on output, investment, and exports. Historical data spanning four decades indicates that increased productivity does not inherently lead to higher wages. The critical factor is a labour market characterised by worker scarcity, which enhances their value. Achieving this condition is the pivotal challenge India now confronts.

(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)
